_README: Musical content for the genre learning paths. It is written to be accurate, but "verified": false means it has not had a final human review — flip it to true once you've checked a genre. This file is plain data; edit freely.

genres.name: Blues
genres.blurb: Dominant 7th chords, the 12-bar form, and expressive minor-pentatonic / blues-scale soloing.

lessons.title: The blues feel: dominant 7th chords
lessons.explainer: Blues harmony leans on dominant 7th chords (root, 3rd, 5th, ♭7) for the I, IV and V — where most pop would use plain major triads. That flat 7th is what gives the blues its restless, bittersweet edge.
lessons.practice: Play E7, A7 and B7, switching between them in time and listening for the ♭7 in each.

lessons.title: Minor pentatonic & the blue note
lessons.explainer: The minor pentatonic (E G A B D) is the core of blues lead playing. Adding the ♭5 turns it into the six-note blues scale — that extra 'blue note' is usually bent into or passed through quickly for tension.
lessons.practice: Run the E blues scale up and down around the 12th-fret box, bending into the ♭5.

lessons.title: The 12-bar form
lessons.explainer: The 12-bar blues is the genre's signature form: three four-bar phrases built from the I, IV and V chords. Once it's in your ears you can trade choruses with almost any blues musician.
lessons.practice: Comp through the 12-bar form slowly, then bring it up to a shuffle tempo.

lessons.title: Open tunings for slide
lessons.explainer: Open G (D G D G B D) tunes the open strings to a G major chord, so a single barre gives you a full chord anywhere on the neck — the classic setup for slide blues.
lessons.practice: Tune to Open G, strum the open strings, then barre straight across at the 5th and 7th frets.

genres.name: Rock
genres.blurb: Power chords, driving rhythms, Drop D riffs, and pentatonic / Mixolydian leads.

lessons.title: Power chords
lessons.explainer: A power chord is just the root and 5th — no 3rd — so it's neither major nor minor. That ambiguity stays clean and punchy under distortion, and the same shape slides anywhere on the neck.
lessons.practice: Play E5, A5 and D5 with palm muting for a tight, percussive rock rhythm.

lessons.title: Drop D power
lessons.explainer: Dropping the low E string to D lets you fret a power chord with one finger across the bottom three strings, and gives a heavier, lower root — the backbone of countless rock and metal riffs.
lessons.practice: Tune to Drop D and play one-finger power chords by barring the low three strings at frets 0, 3 and 5.

lessons.title: The Mixolydian ♭VII
lessons.explainer: Borrowing the ♭VII chord (D in the key of E) comes from the Mixolydian mode and gives that wide-open, classic-rock sound. The ♭VII–IV–I cadence sidesteps the leading tone, so it feels anthemic rather than tense.
lessons.practice: Loop E–D–A and feel how the ♭VII relaxes back toward the tonic.

lessons.title: Pentatonic soloing
lessons.explainer: The minor pentatonic is the default vocabulary for rock leads — five notes that sit well over both minor and dominant backing. Learn one box, then connect the boxes up the neck.
lessons.practice: Solo over an E–D–A vamp using only the E minor pentatonic, landing on chord tones on the downbeats.

genres.name: Folk
genres.blurb: Open chords, fingerpicking-friendly tunings like DADGAD, and singer-songwriter progressions.

lessons.title: Open chords: G, C, D
lessons.explainer: Open-position G, C and D ring with unfretted strings, giving folk its bright, resonant strum. They're the first chords most players learn and the foundation of thousands of songs.
lessons.practice: Change cleanly between G, C and D in a steady down-up strum without stopping.

lessons.title: The G major scale
lessons.explainer: The G major scale (G A B C D E F#) tells you which notes and chords belong together in the key of G, so you can add melodic fills between chords and understand why folk progressions use the chords they do.
lessons.practice: Play the G major scale in open position, naming each scale degree as you go.

lessons.title: The four-chord song
lessons.explainer: I–V–vi–IV (G–D–Em–C) is the four-chord engine behind a huge share of folk and pop songs. The vi adds a touch of melancholy before IV leads back home.
lessons.practice: Loop G–D–Em–C and try singing a melody over the changes.

lessons.title: DADGAD: the modal folk tuning
lessons.explainer: DADGAD (D A D G A D) lowers the 1st, 2nd and 6th strings so the open strings form a droning Dsus4 — neither major nor minor. It's prized in Celtic and modern fingerstyle folk for its ringing, modal character.
lessons.practice: Tune to DADGAD, let the open strings ring, then explore simple one- and two-finger shapes up the neck.

genres.name: Jazz
genres.blurb: Seventh and extended chords, ii–V–I motion, modal improvisation and smooth voice-leading.

lessons.title: The ii–V–I cadence
lessons.explainer: The ii–V–I is the central cadence of jazz: the iim7 sets up the dominant V7, whose tritone pulls strongly into the Imaj7. Hearing and voicing this motion smoothly is the heart of jazz harmony.
lessons.practice: Comp Dm7–G7–Cmaj7, keeping common tones and moving the inner voices as little as possible.

lessons.title: Major 7th: the resting sound
lessons.explainer: A major 7th chord (1-3-5-7) sounds lush and at rest — the home color of a major key in jazz, far warmer and more open than a plain triad.
lessons.practice: Play Cmaj7 and let it ring, then compare its sound directly to a plain C major triad.

lessons.title: Dorian over the ii chord
lessons.explainer: Over a iim7 chord, the Dorian mode (D E F G A B C — a minor scale with a natural 6th) outlines the chord tones and gives that smooth, cool minor color jazz players favor.
lessons.practice: Improvise over a Dm7 vamp using D Dorian, landing on the chord tones D, F, A and C.

lessons.title: Mixolydian over the V chord
lessons.explainer: Mixolydian (G A B C D E F — major with a ♭7) is the basic scale over a dominant V7, spelling out its root, 3rd, 5th and ♭7 and leading naturally into the tonic.
lessons.practice: Play G Mixolydian over a G7 vamp, then resolve smoothly to the 3rd of Cmaj7.

genres.name: Metal
genres.blurb: Down-tuned power chords, palm-muted riffing, and dark scales like Phrygian and harmonic minor.

lessons.title: Palm-muted power chords
lessons.explainer: Metal is built on power chords driven by tight palm muting — resting the picking-hand edge near the bridge to choke the strings into a percussive chug. With no 3rd, they stay clear and aggressive under heavy distortion.
lessons.practice: Palm-mute E5 in steady eighth or sixteenth notes, then accent off-beats for a galloping rhythm.

lessons.title: Down-tuning: Drop C
lessons.explainer: Drop C (C G C F A D) takes Drop D down a further whole step: lower, heavier, and still one-finger power chords on the bottom strings. The looser string tension also makes for chunkier palm mutes.
lessons.practice: Tune to Drop C and play one-finger power chords low on the neck, focusing on tight muting between hits.

lessons.title: The Phrygian mode
lessons.explainer: Phrygian (E F G A B C D — minor with a ♭2) is a metal staple: that half-step between the root and ♭2 sounds instantly dark and menacing.
lessons.practice: Riff around the open low strings using E Phrygian, leaning on the F (♭2) for tension.

lessons.title: The Phrygian i–♭II move
lessons.explainer: The i–♭II move (Em–F) is the sound of Phrygian metal — the ♭II chord sits a half step above the tonic for maximum darkness and menace.
lessons.practice: Chug Em, then shift up a half step to F, palm-muting both and accenting the change.

genres.name: Funk
genres.blurb: Tight sixteenth-note muting, dominant 9th chords, and single-note minor-pentatonic grooves.

lessons.title: The dominant 9th 'chank'
lessons.explainer: Funk rhythm guitar lives on the dominant 9th (1-3-5-♭7-9), played with crisp sixteenth-note strumming and lots of fretting-hand muting for that scratchy 'chank'. The chord barely changes — the groove does the work.
lessons.practice: Strum E9 in tight sixteenths, muting most strokes with the fretting hand and letting only the accents ring.

lessons.title: Single-note pentatonic grooves
lessons.explainer: Single-note funk lines lean on the minor pentatonic, played staccato and locked to the sixteenth-note grid. Space and rhythm matter as much as the notes you choose.
lessons.practice: Play short, punchy E-minor-pentatonic phrases over a one-chord vamp, leaving rests on the off-beats for a tight pocket.

lessons.title: Riding a two-chord vamp
lessons.explainer: Much of funk sits on a two-chord vamp rather than a moving progression. Em7 to A7 outlines E Dorian (minor with a natural 6th), giving a bright, groovy minor color to ride for whole sections.
lessons.practice: Vamp Em7–A7 in sixteenths and drop short fills between the chords.

lessons.title: Dorian color for solos
lessons.explainer: E Dorian (E F# G A B C# D) is the go-to scale over a minor funk vamp — the natural 6th (C#) adds lift and brightness compared with a plain minor scale.
lessons.practice: Solo over an Em7 vamp using E Dorian, targeting the natural 6th to bring out the Dorian flavor.
